# Pesher Psalms (4Q171, 4Q173) — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Manuscripts** | 4Q171 (4QPsa), 4Q173 (4QPsb), Cave 4, Qumran |
| **Language** | Hebrew |
| **Date of Composition** | c. 1st century BCE |
| **Genre** | Pesher — sectarian biblical commentary (continuous) |
| **Base Texts** | Primarily Psalm 37; fragments of Psalms 45, 60, 127, 129 |
| **Extent** | 5 columns (4Q171), 5 small fragments (4Q173), fragmentary |
| **In One Sentence** | A Qumran commentary on Psalm 37 that reads the psalmist's meditation on the righteous and the wicked as a precise prophecy about the Teacher of Righteousness, his enemies, and the community's future inheritance of the land. |

---

## Sections Overview

Like all continuous pesharim, the text follows its base text lemma by lemma. 4Q171 is the primary and more substantial manuscript; 4Q173 preserves smaller fragments covering Psalms 127 and 129 and possibly others.

- **Columns 1–3 (4Q171)**: Continuous commentary on Psalm 37:7–26, with identifications of "the wicked" as various enemies of the community and "the righteous" as the Teacher of Righteousness and his followers.
- **Column 4 (4Q171)**: Commentary on Psalm 37:28–40, including a crucial passage on the Teacher's confrontation with the Wicked Priest, and the fate of the enemies on the "Day of Vengeance."
- **Column 5 (fragmentary)**: Commentary extending into other psalms; the surviving 4Q171 fragment covers Psalm 45 with a messianic interpretation.
- **4Q173 fragments**: Cover Psalms 127 and 129, each following the standard lemma + "its interpretation concerns..." format.

---

## The World Behind the Text

Psalm 37 is one of the Hebrew Bible's great wisdom psalms — an alphabetic acrostic poem (each pair of verses begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet) meditating on a perennial problem: why do the wicked prosper and the righteous suffer? The psalm's answer is patience and trust: "Do not fret because of evildoers... For they will soon wither like grass." The wicked will be cut off; the meek will inherit the land; the righteous will be vindicated.

This was a perfect psalm for the Qumran community to interpret. They believed themselves to be precisely the righteous who were suffering under precisely the wicked. The psalm's promises — "the meek shall inherit the land" (v. 11), "the wicked lie in wait for the righteous and seek to kill him, but the LORD will not leave him in their power" (vv. 32–33) — resonated with the community's experience of conflict, exile, and persecution.

The social world of the text is the same as all the pesharim: the late Hasmonean period, probably the 1st century BCE. The primary antagonists in 4Q171 are the figures known from other Scrolls as the **Wicked Priest** and the **Man of the Lie**. These are code names, and their historical identification has been debated for decades.

**The Wicked Priest** (ha-kohen ha-rasha') is widely understood to be one of the Hasmonean priest-kings — the most common candidates are Jonathan Maccabaeus (152–143 BCE) or his brother Simon (143–134 BCE), who assumed the high priesthood in the Hasmonean period in ways the Qumran community regarded as illegitimate. (Some scholars prefer John Hyrcanus or Alexander Jannaeus.) Pesher Psalms describes the Wicked Priest as a man who pursued the Teacher of Righteousness to his place of exile to afflict him on the Day of Atonement — a stunning detail that implies a violent confrontation on the holiest day of the year.

**The Man of the Lie** (ish ha-kazav) appears to be a different figure — possibly a leader within the broader Jewish community (or even within the movement itself) who rejected the Teacher's authority and led others astray. In 4Q171, the Man of the Lie is associated with those who "preach lies" and lead the community of the poor astray.

**The Teacher of Righteousness** (moreh ha-tzedeq) is the community's founder and authoritative interpreter — the figure who received the true meaning of the prophets from God. Psalm 37:32 ("the wicked lie in wait for the righteous and seek to kill him") is interpreted as referring specifically to the Teacher and the Wicked Priest. The Teacher's fate — whether he was killed or died naturally — is not stated in the Scrolls with certainty, though Pesher Psalms implies violence was attempted.

---

## Why This Text Was Written

The pesher on Psalm 37 was written for the same reason all pesharim were written: to confirm that the community's situation was not accidental, not a sign of divine abandonment, but the fulfillment of ancient prophecy. If the righteous suffers now, the psalmist already promised vindication. If the wicked prospers now, the psalmist already promised their destruction.

More specifically, 4Q171 addresses the community's persistent anxiety about **the land**. Psalm 37 returns seven times to the inheritance of the land ("the meek shall inherit the land," vv. 9, 11, 22, 29, 34). For a community that had separated itself from Jerusalem — either voluntarily or by expulsion — and retreated to the Judean desert, the promise of land inheritance was charged with immediate meaning. The pesher interprets "the meek shall inherit the land" as a promise that the community will eventually repossess the promised inheritance currently controlled by their enemies.

The text also provides a theodicy — an answer to the question of why righteous people suffer. The answer is not general wisdom but specific prophecy: the suffering is known to God, the enemies are named in scripture, and the outcome is guaranteed.

---

## How to Read This Text

Begin by reading all of Psalm 37 straight through. It is a relatively long psalm, but coherent: the righteous/wicked contrast is sustained through the entire poem. Note the recurring phrases — "do not fret," "trust in the LORD," "the meek/poor shall inherit the land," "wait for the LORD." These are the phrases the pesherist will key on.

Then read 4Q171 alongside the psalm, column by column. The technique is mechanical in one sense — lemma, interpretation, lemma, interpretation — but the identifications make it politically electric. Every "righteous man" in the psalm becomes the Teacher of Righteousness or the community. Every "wicked man" becomes the Wicked Priest or the Man of the Lie or the "congregation of the Seekers of Smooth Things" (the Pharisees). Every promise of inheritance becomes a prophecy about the community's future restoration.

Pay special attention to the column 4 material on Psalm 37:32–33 — the Wicked Priest pursuing the Teacher to his "house of exile" to swallow him on the Day of Atonement. This is one of the most vivid and specific historical allusions in all the pesharim. It implies that the Wicked Priest tracked down the Teacher's community on Yom Kippur — a day when the community was fasting and observing their own calendar — and attacked or confronted him. The calendar dispute between Qumran and Jerusalem means the two groups observed Yom Kippur on different days; the Wicked Priest's ability to travel on that day (when Jerusalem was keeping Yom Kippur on a different date) is what made the attack possible.

---

## The Threads — How This Text Connects

**Psalm 37:11** — "the meek shall inherit the land" (Hebrew: *anavim*). This verse is interpreted by the pesherist as a promise to the Qumran community. It is also the verse cited in **Matthew 5:5**: "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth." Jesus's Beatitude does not come from thin air — it quotes this psalm. 4Q171 shows that in the very period of Jesus's life, Psalm 37:11 was being read as a promise to the righteous poor who were suffering under corrupt leadership. The community of Qumran applied it to themselves; Jesus applied it to those who followed him. Both are drawing on the same exegetical tradition.

**The Teacher of Righteousness** as a figure who suffers at the hands of the Jerusalem establishment and whose fate involves violence by the Wicked Priest creates — in some scholars' readings — a suggestive background for messianic suffering traditions. This connection should not be overstated: the Scrolls do not call the Teacher a messiah, and his role is as interpreter, not atoner. But the structural parallel of a righteous teacher, rejected by the religious establishment, whose suffering is interpreted as prophetically significant, is part of the wider Second Temple landscape that shapes NT messianism.

**Psalm 45** (the "royal wedding psalm," an explicit superscription), fragments of which are preserved in 4Q171, receives a messianic interpretation at Qumran. The psalm's address to a king ("your throne, O God, is forever and ever") was read by later Jewish and Christian interpreters as messianic or even divine. Hebrews 1:8–9 quotes Psalm 45:6–7 as a direct address to the Son. The Qumran messianic interpretation of Psalm 45 predates the NT use and shows a common exegetical tradition.

**Habakkuk Pesher (1QpHab)** is the most complete and famous of all pesharim, covering the first two chapters of Habakkuk. It describes the same core dramatis personae — Teacher of Righteousness, Wicked Priest, Man of the Lie — and should be read alongside 4Q171 for a fuller picture of the community's self-understanding.

**Matthew 5:5** — see above. The connection between 4Q171's interpretation of Psalm 37:11 and the Beatitude in the Sermon on the Mount is one of the most striking convergences between the Dead Sea Scrolls and the New Testament.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

- **Psalm 37 is an acrostic.** Every two verses begin with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph (v. 1–2) to tav (v. 39–40). The pesherist is commenting on a carefully constructed literary-theological poem, not a random collection of sayings. The acrostic structure signals completeness — the righteous/wicked contrast is meant to cover the full alphabet, the full range of human experience. A reader of the Hebrew text would feel this structure; a reader in translation mostly loses it.

- **"Inherit the land" is politically explosive, not merely spiritual.** Modern readers may hear "inherit the earth" (the NT version) as a vague spiritual promise. In its original context — both in the psalm and in the pesher — "the land" means the land of Israel, the covenantal territory. For a community in desert exile, this was an intensely concrete, politically charged promise. The pesher is not offering a spiritualized afterlife hope; it is promising literal political and territorial restoration.

- **The Day of Atonement confrontation is the most personal detail in all the pesharim.** No other text gives us an image as specific as the Wicked Priest crossing into enemy territory on a holy day to confront the Teacher. This suggests a historical event — a real moment — that the community preserved and interpreted. What actually happened during that confrontation is unknown; the text implies violence or at least grave threat. The fact that it was remembered in these terms says something about how the community experienced its founding trauma.

- **The Man of the Lie and the Wicked Priest are different enemies.** Beginning readers often conflate them. The Wicked Priest is a priestly-political figure in Jerusalem — someone with institutional power. The Man of the Lie appears to be a teacher or leader who was once close to the community or to the Teacher's movement but who defected or distorted the message. These are two separate crises: external priestly opposition and internal doctrinal betrayal.

- **"The congregation of the poor" (adat ha-evyonim)** is a term the community uses for itself in this pesher. It links to the biblical tradition of the *anawim* (the poor, the meek, the humble) who trust in God rather than in earthly power — a tradition that also feeds the Beatitudes and the spirituality of Luke's Gospel. The Qumran community understood their material poverty and political marginalization as theological identity markers.

- **We do not know the Teacher of Righteousness's name.** After decades of scholarship, no consensus has emerged. The Scrolls are careful to use his title, never his name. This may be reverential discretion, or it may be that his name was too well-known to need stating — and therefore lost to us once the community itself vanished.

---

## Why This Text Isn't in Your Bible

Pesher Psalms is a sectarian commentary, not scripture. Like all the pesharim, it was never a candidate for any canon — it is one community's interpretation of texts that are themselves canonical. Its preservation in Cave 4 was accidental; its survival across two millennia is a function of Judean desert conditions.

The Qumran community, which produced this text, did not survive the Roman-Jewish War (66–73 CE). The settlement at Qumran was destroyed c. 68 CE by Roman forces. With the community went the living tradition of interpretation that made texts like 4Q171 comprehensible from the inside. What survived were the scrolls themselves, hidden in the caves — a library that outlasted the community that created it by two thousand years.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| c. 150–140 BCE | Likely founding period of the Qumran community; Teacher of Righteousness active |
| 152–143 BCE | Jonathan Maccabaeus serves as High Priest (primary candidate for "Wicked Priest") |
| 143–134 BCE | Simon Maccabaeus as High Priest and Ethnarch (alternative candidate) |
| c. 1st century BCE | Composition of Pesher Psalms (4Q171, 4Q173) |
| c. 68 CE | Roman destruction of Qumran; Scrolls hidden in caves |
| 1947–1956 CE | Discovery and excavation of Cave 4; recovery of 4Q171 fragments |
| 1968 CE | J. M. Allegro publishes 4Q171 in Discoveries in the Judaean Desert V |

---
